Listen to a talk in a biology class.

Today I want to look at camouflage, and I'll describe three different strategies, because students often mix them up. The first is background matching. Here, an animal's color simply matches its surroundings. The snowshoe hare is a nice example. Its coat is brown in summer, but it turns white in winter, so it matches the snow. The second strategy is called disruptive coloration. These animals don't match the background at all. Instead, they have bold patterns, like stripes or spots, that break up the outline of the body. A zebra's stripes are the classic case. When zebras stand together, a predator has trouble seeing where one animal ends and the next begins. The third strategy is mimicry. In mimicry, a harmless animal looks like a dangerous one. For instance, the hoverfly has yellow and black bands, so birds mistake it for a wasp and leave it alone, even though the hoverfly can't sting at all. So, matching, breaking up the outline, and imitating something dangerous. Keep those three separate.
Listen to a talk in an economics class.

Economists usually divide unemployment into three types, and each one has a different cause. Let's start with frictional unemployment. This is the short period when people are between jobs. Say a graduate is looking for her first position, or someone quits to find a better job. A certain amount of frictional unemployment is actually a sign of a healthy economy, because it means people feel free to move. Structural unemployment is different. It happens when workers' skills no longer match the jobs that are available. For example, when a factory installs automated machines, some workers lose their jobs, and if they don't have, say, computer skills, they can't easily find new work. This kind can last for years. And finally, cyclical unemployment. This is caused by the business cycle. During a recession, people buy less, so overall demand falls, and companies lay off workers. The good news is that cyclical unemployment usually goes down when the economy recovers. So remember: between jobs, skills mismatch, and falling demand.
Listen to a talk in a psychology class.

Psychologists often describe memory as three connected systems. The first is sensory memory. It takes in a huge amount of information from our eyes and ears, but it holds that information for only about a second. Most of it simply disappears. If we pay attention to something, it moves into short-term memory. Short-term memory can hold only a small number of items, about seven, and only for around twenty seconds unless we keep repeating them. Think about the last time someone told you a phone number. You probably repeated it to yourself until you could dial it, and then it was gone. That's short-term memory at work. Finally, there's long-term memory. Its capacity seems to be practically unlimited, and information can stay there for years, even a lifetime. Getting information into long-term memory usually requires connecting it to things we already know.
Listen to a talk in an ecology class.

When two species live in close contact, we call it symbiosis. But symbiosis comes in three forms, depending on who benefits. In mutualism, both partners benefit. Clownfish and sea anemones are a good example. The anemone's stinging tentacles protect the clownfish from predators, and the clownfish, in return, chases away fish that would eat the anemone. In commensalism, one species benefits and the other is basically unaffected. Barnacles attach themselves to the skin of whales. The barnacles get a free ride to waters full of food, and the whale doesn't really gain or lose anything. Then there's parasitism. Here one species benefits at the expense of the other. A tick feeding on a deer's blood is a parasite. Notice that both commensal organisms and parasites live on their hosts. The difference is whether the host is harmed.

Listen to a talk in an ecology class.

People often assume that the most important species in an ecosystem is the most common one. But ecologists use the term keystone species for something different. A keystone species refers to a species whose effect on its ecosystem is much larger than its numbers would suggest. The classic example comes from the coast of Washington State. A researcher removed a type of sea star from a stretch of rocky shore. The sea stars weren't very numerous, but they ate mussels. Without them, the mussels took over the rocks, crowded out other species, and the number of species in the area dropped by more than half. So a keystone isn't the biggest or the most common piece. It's the one that holds the structure together.
Listen to a talk in a history class.

Let's talk about the printing press. Johannes Gutenberg developed his press with movable metal type around 1440, in the German city of Mainz. Before that, books in Europe were copied by hand, which made them rare and expensive. Gutenberg's most famous project, a printed Bible, was finished around 1455. The technology spread quickly. By the year 1500, printers in more than two hundred European cities had produced an estimated twenty million books. Cheaper books meant that more people learned to read, and new ideas could travel far faster than before.
Listen to a talk in an Earth science class.

Ask people why we have seasons, and many will say it's because Earth is closer to the sun in summer. That's a common idea, but it's wrong. In fact, Earth is slightly closer to the sun in January, which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere. The primary reason for the seasons is the tilt of Earth's axis, about twenty-three and a half degrees. When your hemisphere is tilted toward the sun, sunlight hits the ground more directly and the days are longer, so it's summer. When it's tilted away, the light is spread out and the days are short. Distance plays only a very small role.
